core: Time complexity describes how an algorithm's running time GROWS as the input size n grows, not the wall-clock time on a particular machine
The analysis method: count basic operations as a function of n, keep the dominant term, drop constant factors and lower-order terms
Big-O notation and its formal meaning: f(n) is O(g(n)) if there are positive constants c and k with 0 <= f(n) <= c*g(n) for all n >= k
The common complexity classes and their ordering: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n^2) < O(2^n)
Best, average, and worst case, and that Big-O typically expresses a worst-case upper bound
That Big-O is an upper bound; Big-Omega is a lower bound and Big-Theta a tight bound (named briefly)
One worked example counting operations: a nested-loop pair scan performs n(n-1)/2 comparisons, which is O(n^2)
supporting: History: the O symbol was introduced by Paul Bachmann (1894) and popularized by Edmund Landau (hence 'Landau symbols'); Donald Knuth standardized O, Omega, and Theta for algorithm analysis in computer science (1976)
Concrete anchoring examples drawn from sibling topics (array index O(1), linear scan O(n), binary search O(log n), dictionary lookup O(1) average) cited only as illustrations
Why growth rate matters more than constants for large inputs
outOfScope: Space complexity - the memory analog - which is its own sibling topic (named in one sentence and handed off)
Teaching specific searching or sorting algorithms in detail (own sibling topics); their complexities are cited only as examples
Amortized analysis and the master theorem for recurrences (beyond an introductory lesson)

claims.claim: Time complexity measures how the number of basic operations an algorithm performs grows as a function of the input size n, abstracting away hardware and language so the same analysis holds across machines.
Big-O notation gives an asymptotic upper bound: f(n) = O(g(n)) means there are positive constants c and k such that 0 <= f(n) <= c*g(n) for all n >= k.
claims.verification: Definition quoted from NIST DADS 'big-O notation' entry, read 2026-08-19.

claims.claim: In analysis we keep the dominant term and drop constant factors and lower-order terms: an algorithm doing 3n + 5 operations is O(n), and a nested double loop doing n(n-1)/2 comparisons is O(n^2).
claims.verification: Verified in Python 3 via Bash on 2026-08-19: nested-loop comparison count equals n(n-1)/2 for n in {1,2,5,8,10}; the linear sum over [3,9,2,7,5] performs exactly 5 additions and returns 26.

claims.claim: The standard complexity classes grow in the strict order O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n^2) < O(2^n); at n = 1024, log2(n) = 10, n = 1024, n*log2(n) = 10240, and n^2 = 1048576.
claims.verification: Growth values and the strictly-increasing ordering computed in Python 3 via Bash on 2026-08-19.

claims.claim: An algorithm can have different best-, average-, and worst-case running times; a linear one-by-one scan of n items is O(1) best case (target first) and O(n) worst case (target last or absent), and Big-O usually reports the worst case.
Big-O is an upper bound; Big-Omega expresses a lower bound and Big-Theta a tight (matching upper and lower) bound. Because O is only an upper bound, an O(n) algorithm is also technically O(n^2).

A Python dictionary (hash map) lookup is O(1) on average but O(n) in the worst case when hash collisions are frequent; average-case timings assume a hash function robust enough that collisions are uncommon.
claims.verification: Values and the collision caveat taken from the official Python wiki TimeComplexity table, read 2026-08-19.

claims.claim: The O symbol was introduced by the number theorist Paul Bachmann in 1894 (in Analytische Zahlentheorie), and adopted and popularized by Edmund Landau, so O and o are called Landau symbols.

Donald Knuth established the standard use of O, Omega, and Theta in computer science in his 1976 SIGACT News note 'Big Omicron and Big Omega and Big Theta,' which also corrected the loose habit of writing O(n^2) for a lower bound when Omega was meant.

sourceRecords.notes: Read 2026-08-19. Authoritative, public-domain definition of big-O as an asymptotic upper bound: 'f(n) = O(g(n)) means there are positive constants c and k, such that 0 <= f(n) <= cg(n) for all n >= k.' Links to Big-Theta, Big-Omega, little-o, and complexity, and notes O is an upper bound frequently misused to mean equality. Supports the formal definition, the upper-bound framing, and the naming of Theta/Omega. Prose synthesized, not copied.
